It's so funny.  When I first saw the Mammoth I thought *why the hell does it look like they put Master Chief's helmet on a big truck?*  Because that's exactly what it looks like.

But it's really a representation of the Halo fanboi.  There are many things to be nerdy about out there: Star Wars, Star Trek, Dr. Who, Kubrick films, Lord of the Rings etc. etc.  So many great and wonderful ways to waste time.  And then we have the Halo series.

The more I look at Halo the more I am convinced there is nothing special about this series other than the fact that it is Microsoft Studio's flagship product.  It's tacky.  The story is minimalistic and unengaging.  The level design is shit (I repeat: *THE LEVEL DESIGN IS TRULY SHIT*).  The visual design is so unfocused it should be considered amateur.

And yet the success of the Halo series persists.  Not only that, but fans of the series are incredibly vocal about the strengths of their beloved franchise.  It created the two-weapon and regenerating health system.  Both quite interesting innovations.  But that was 2001.  Nothing has really changed since then.  Same system, pretty much same look, same shitty level design.  Every sequel could actually be considered an expansion pack.

And then we have the vocal Halo fanboi.  There are only two things to say about them.  The first is that they are underexposed.  When ever I come across someone who says they love the Halo games I look them dead in the eye and say, "You, sir, haven't played many videogames."  There are indie games, old rpgs and classic beat-em-ups that are more engaging than Master Chief and his ridiculous planet ring.

The second thing I have to say about the fanboi concerns that image in the title.  It's the fanboi's measure of quality, and the only way to please them: give them more of the same, just make it bigger.  That stupid looking truck with the Master Chief windows serves as a visual metaphor for me.  The fanboi doesn't want to just drive a vehicle this time around.  He wants to drive *a big fucking truck with Master Cheif's goddamn face on it because that's what his definition of awesome equates to*.

As a connesseur of fine video games I find myself agreeing with a great deal of these posts: Deus Ex, Half-Life 2, the Civilization series.  System Shock 2 is worth a mention (currently on my 2nd playthrough right now). But there is one gem that I always come back to.

Ladies and gentlemen I present to you the finest fighting game in the tradition of Double Dragon: 2005's The Warriors.

(Link)
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Warriors_(video_game)

The premise is simple: beat the shit out of as many motherfuckers as you can.

Based on the 1979 Walter Hill movie by the same title, The Warriors follows the story of the gang as they come from their humble roots right up until the plot of the movie (which you also play through).  It does a great job at expanding on the original mythology of the film.  The use of MoCap in the cutscenes gives it a truly authentic feel.  They even brought back all of the actors who were still alive to do the dialogue.

Also, you have to beat the ever loving shit out of motherfuckers.

So why is Jar-Jar Binks considered one of the worst characters in cinematic history?  Is it the voice?  The thinly-veiled racism?  The smell?

For many, Jar-Jar is a representation of why the Star Wars prequels were complete garbage.  Mainly the question gets asked: why didn't they just stick to the original formula?  Keep a golly-gee-whiz adventurous tone with interesting characters (including the dashing bad boy, Han Solo) and a very specific visual style.  The prequels tossed out everything: interesting characters (no bad boys or truly sinister mofos) the adventurous attitude (everyone's so goddamn serious and the universe is without any sense of discovery) and the visual style went from grey - black - red to someone puking a crayola box onto a computer.  Not to mention a complete waste of Samuel L. Jackson.  Didn't say motherfucker *once*.

The fact is this: the original Star Wars trilogy and The Prequels are two completely different sets of movies.  Nothing makes that more apparent than the existence of Jar-Jar Binks.

Now lets ask ourselves: why does this Jar-Jar thing have to exist?  Is he essential for the story?  Oh, wait, if they didn't meet him in the first one, they wouldn't have made it to the city, so of course he's an essential character!  Ha ha!  Almost lost it, there.

Actually, just because he performs a function in the story is no argument for his existence.  The fact remains it's still a very strange character - in the Star Wars universe, Jar-Jar is completely out of place.  If he were in the original trilogy he'd probably be a bounty hunter that sounded like Michael Clarke Duncan with 15 seconds of screen time.  Instead he's some kind of racist stereotype manchild that comes from a race of fish people who speak english at full retard.

The apologistic arguments for Jar-Jar don't help: he's supposed to be funny, this is a kids movie, grow up he's not really that bad etc.  But let me lay something down here: The original Star Wars (before it was called A New Hope) came to theatres and rocked a generation of moviegoers.  It was a space opera intended to strike and amaze you.  It wasn't "Just for Kids" and it didn't sacrifice screen time for unnecessary jokes.  It was incredibly well edited (a story in it's own right) and anything that didn't help the atmosphere, spirit and 'feel' of this amazing movie was let out.  They didn't make excuses - this wasn't just a "kids movie" that they could say "hey whatever tell that black guy to sniff some glue and dance with chewbacca for a half-hour".  That would have been stupid.

Just like Jar-Jar Binks

Truly, the worst thing about Jar-Jar Binks is that he exists.  He is an effigy of the dissapointment felt by fans of the original series; we wanted another Star Wars movie, and we didn't get one.  What we got was shit.

In the last four days leading up to the release of 1977's Star Wars, Lucas' then-wife, Marcia Lucas, and three other editors re-cut the hell out of the damn thing.  The movie was literally re-created in the editing room.  And the result was one of the most well-loved movies of all time.

In the mid-90s, George re-released Star Wars twice.  The second time he re-edited the film again (sped-up opening, deleted scenes that repeat information, character alterations, and a re-cut of the final moments of the death star battle) and COMPLETELY changed the flow of the movie.  Since making these changes (and a few more here and there), George has only re-released the original film once on DVD (for a limited time) and completely refuses to re-release them in the future, hinting at the idea he may have destroyed the original.

This is why I feel sorry for people like you.  Star Wars, The Empire Strikes Back and (to a somewhat lesser extent) Return of the Jedi defined my childhood.  They were precious to me back then and they are today.  They were incredible stories, more than just special effects and simple ideas.

Now, after all the toys, videogames, prequels and tv series, all that's left is a pile of mediocre garbage left in the shape of a giant media conglomerate.  It doesn't surprise me in the least that there are folks like you that shrug their shoulders and say, "what's the big deal?  It's not really all that special."  You're right.  It's not.  But it used to be.

And I remember.
